On the moon Orthe, beneath a dim orange sun, a Veyr drifts above the floor of an ammonia-dark ocean. It is about forty metres across, but only a few metres thick. Between the plates run branching channels of fluid. Some carry dissolved metals; others hold chemicals that would react violently if mixed. When it is no longer needed, the region dissolves and its materials are carried elsewhere.

There are no cells in the familiar sense. Its living machinery is a mesh of repeating chemical reactions, each enclosed by a membrane-thin boundary. The Veyr stays alive by keeping those reactions going—and by continually rebuilding the boundaries that keep them in order.

It has no mouth. The whole of its underside absorbs and processes the ocean around it. Where warm mineral-rich water seeps from the seabed, the Veyr spreads out its plates and draws the chemicals through its pores. Where the water is poor in useful compounds, it contracts into a thicker, narrower shape and drifts on the slow currents. It does not swim. It changes the chemistry around itself, causing one edge to become buoyant while another grows heavier.
